content.title: About
content.content: Sirloin beef steak is a lean cut taken from the back of the cow. It offers a tender flavor, moderate fat content, and a satisfying texture. The NS (no‑salt) version is unseasoned, allowing the natural taste of the meat to shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sirloin is one of the most popular cuts for steaks because of its balance of tenderness and flavor.
Beef provides all essential amino acids required by humans.
Traditionally, sirloin is grilled, pan‑seared, or roasted at high heat.
Its fat content is generally lower than ribeye or New York strip.
The cut is known as “sirloin” in the US and UK, and often called “вырезка” in Russian.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100 g serving delivers about 26 g of high‑quality protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is highly bioavailable, and zinc, which supports immune function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Sirloin is abundant in vitamin B12, niacin (B3), and riboflavin (B2), all important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Low in added fat
items.content: The NS version has minimal added fat, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Supports muscle mass
items.content: High protein and amino acid content help maintain and build muscle, especially with regular exercise.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor harmful bacteria such as E. coli. Cook steak to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Beef contains purines, which can raise uric acid levels in people prone to gout.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rare, but some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Sodium in processed versions
items.content: While NS is unsalted, pre‑marinated products can add significant sodium.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sirloin steak is best cooked over high heat—grill, cast‑iron skillet, or oven—reaching your preferred doneness (rare, medium, well‑done). Let the steak rest at room temperature for 20‑30 minutes before cooking and rest 5‑10 minutes after cooking so juices redistribute. Serve with vegetables, herbs, or a light sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh steak refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the refrigerator, not at room temperature, before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Bread, whole grain white, toasted is a whole‑grain white bread made from wheat flour that has been lightly toasted to a golden crust. It retains the characteristic aroma of toasted bread while staying soft inside and providing the nutrients of whole grain.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain bread contains all parts of the grain: bran, germ and endosperm.
Toasting enhances aroma and creates a crispier crust.
In many cultures toasted bread is used as a base for open‑face sandwiches and snacks.
Thermal processing can slightly reduce some vitamin levels but preserves most dietary fiber.
Bread is often served with butter, cheese, or avocado to boost flavor and nutrition.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain bread provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains thiamine, niacin and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The bread supplies iron, magnesium and zinc, important for blood formation and immunity.

items.title: Lower glycemic index than white bread
items.content: Whole‑grain bread raises blood sugar more slowly, beneficial for glucose control.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of fiber and complex carbs helps you feel full longer.

items.title: Wheat allergy or celiac disease
items.content: People with wheat allergy or celiac disease should avoid this product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some toasted breads contain added salt; monitor intake if you watch sodium.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While less calorie‑dense than white bread, portions should still be moderate.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Certain brands may include preservatives or flavor enhancers that not everyone tolerates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Toasted whole‑grain bread works well for open‑face sandwiches, avocado toast, cheese melts, spreads or as a side for soups. Lightly brush with olive oil or use as a crunchy topping for casseroles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bread in a cool, dry place in a paper bag or bread box. For longer storage, freeze slices and toast them directly from frozen.

content.title: About
content.content: Pineapple upside-down cake is a classic American dessert in which caramelized pineapple rings and cherries are placed at the bottom of the pan, then a vanilla batter is poured over them. After baking, the cake is inverted so the fruit “crust” becomes the top layer, giving the dessert a bright aroma and juicy flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cake first appeared in the United States in the early 1920s and quickly became popular because of its simplicity.
Traditional recipes use canned pineapple, but many bakers prefer fresh pineapple lightly sautéed with brown sugar.
The original version used cherry jam instead of fresh cherries, adding extra sweetness.
It is often served chilled, sometimes with a scoop of vanilla ice cream.
In Japan a variation exists that adds kiwi slices instead of cherries.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Pineapple is rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Bromelain
items.content: The enzyme bromelain found in pineapple helps digestion and has anti‑inflammatory properties.

items.title: Dietary Fiber
items.content: The fruit and whole‑grain batter provide dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Energy Boost
items.content: The cake supplies carbohydrates that quickly replenish energy stores.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It contains potassium and magnesium, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: High Sugar Content
items.content: The cake contains a considerable amount of sugar, so people with diabetes should limit their portion.

items.title: Pineapple Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pineapple, ranging from swelling to itching.

items.title: Caloric Density
items.content: Rich in butter and sugar, the cake is calorie‑dense; moderation is key for weight management.

items.title: Trans Fat
items.content: Using margarine instead of butter can introduce trans fats, which are undesirable for cardiovascular health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the cake in individual slices at room temperature. It can be topped with whipped cream, ice cream, or a dusting of cinnamon. For a fresher taste, add a few slices of fresh pineapple on top.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cake in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. For longer storage, freeze individual portions in a freezer‑safe bag – they retain flavor for up to 2 months. Allow the cake to come to room temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee, pre‑sweetened with sugar, is a ground or instant coffee product that already contains added sugar. It is convenient for quick preparation without the need to add a sweetener separately. The flavor combines the characteristic bitterness of coffee with a gentle sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pre‑sweetened coffee is popular in countries with high consumption of ready‑to‑drink beverages, such as the United States and Japan.
The added sugar helps soften coffee’s acidity and bitterness, making it more appealing to a broad audience.
There are several variants: white sugar, brown sugar, or cane syrup.
Some brands add flavorings (vanilla, caramel) to enhance taste notes.
Instant pre‑sweetened coffee is often used in offices and at events because of its convenience.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: Sugar provides a rapid glucose surge, while coffee stimulates the central nervous system, helping increase alertness.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols, which may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Improved concentration
items.content: Caffeine enhances attention and cognitive performance, especially when consumed in moderate amounts.

items.title: Elevated blood sugar
items.content: Regular consumption of sweetened coffee can raise glucose levels, which is undesirable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Caffeine‑induced anxiety
items.content: High caffeine intake may increase anxiety, insomnia, and heart rate.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can irritate the stomach, especially in individuals with gastritis or ulcer disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dissolve 1‑2 teaspoons in hot water (80‑90 °C) or add to milk. It can also be used in smoothies, desserts, and ice cream to impart a coffee‑sweet flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a sealed package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. For long‑term storage, keep refrigerated to prevent clumping and loss of aroma.

content.title: About
content.content: An empanada is a traditional fried or baked pastry filled with meat, cheese, vegetables or sweet fillings. Product NFS (No. 3470) is sold as ready‑to‑heat portions, vacuum‑sealed for convenience.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Empanadas originate from Spanish and Latin American cuisines, where they are known by many names.
The original dough is made from wheat flour, water, oil and a small amount of yeast.
Fillings can be savory (beef, chicken, cheese) or sweet (apple, ricotta, chocolate).
In Russia empanadas became popular in the 1990s thanks to imported brands.
NFS (3470) is designed for quick microwave preparation in 2–3 minutes.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Meat or cheese fillings provide high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meat fillings are rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough and meat fillings supply vitamins B1, B2, B3 and B6, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Carbohydrates for energy
items.content: Wheat dough delivers quick‑release carbs that give an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: When vegetables are included in the filling, the empanada adds useful fiber for digestion.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Fried empanadas can contain a notable amount of saturated fat, so they should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Ready‑made products often contain added salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: The dough may contain gluten and the fillings dairy; individuals with these allergies should check the label.

items.title: Thermal safety
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave meat fillings undercooked, posing a bacterial risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the empanada in the microwave (or oven) according to the package instructions, then enjoy it hot. It works as a quick snack, a meal, or a side to a salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the sealed package refrigerated at +2…+6 °C. Once opened, consume within 3–4 days. Do not freeze, as it may alter the dough texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Fried eggplant consists of sliced eggplant that is deep‑fried until golden and crisp. The flesh is soft and mildly sweet, while the frying gives it a crunchy texture and rich aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggplant belongs to the nightshade family and is a relative of tomatoes and potatoes.
It is called “aubergine” in British English, “eggplant” in American English, and “brinjal” in South Asia.
The deep purple color comes from anthocyanins, which have antioxidant properties.
Eggplant is a staple in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Asian cuisines.
In many countries fried eggplant is served as a bar snack or in salads.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and vitamin C help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: When eaten in moderation, fried eggplant can fit into a calorie‑controlled diet.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium aids normal blood pressure and heart function.

items.title: Provides vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: High fat content from frying
items.content: Deep‑frying adds calories and saturated fat, which should be limited.

items.title: Nightshade allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggplant.

items.title: Salt and seasoning
items.content: Excessive salt can increase the risk of hypertension.

items.title: Tough skin
items.content: The skin can be hard to digest for people with gastrointestinal issues.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fried eggplant is served hot as an appetizer, in salads, sandwiches, or as a side dish with meat. It pairs well with fresh herbs, lemon juice, or a yogurt‑based sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fried eggplant in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags; it will retain flavor for up to 2 months.

fruit-salad-fresh-or-raw-including-citru.title: Fruit salad, fresh or raw, with citrus fruits, no dressing

content.title: About
content.content: The fruit salad is made from a variety of fresh fruits, including citrus (oranges, mandarins, grapefruit), apples, pears, berries and other seasonal fruits. It is served without any dressing, allowing the natural taste and aroma of the fruits to shine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Citrus fruits are rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system.
Combining different fruits can increase the bioavailability of certain nutrients through enzyme interactions.
Fruit salad is commonly served in the summer season as a refreshing and thirst‑quenching dish.
A salad without dressing retains the natural sweetness of the fruits, adding no extra calories.
The variety of colors and textures makes the dish visually appealing.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Citrus fruits and berries provide high levels of vitamin C, a powerful antioxidant that supports immunity.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fruits such as apples and pears are high in soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: Without added dressing the salad is low in calories, making it suitable for weight management.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: Because fruits have a high water content, they help maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and carotenoids found in berries and citrus protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to citrus fruits, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: High acidity
items.content: Large amounts of citrus can increase stomach acidity and cause discomfort for people with gastritis or reflux.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: If the fruits are not organic, they may carry pesticide residues; thorough washing before consumption is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled; you can add mint or a squeeze of lime for extra aroma. It is eaten with a spoon or fork and can also be used as a side dish for fish or chicken.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours to preserve freshness and texture.

content.title: About
content.content: The Reuben sandwich is a classic American hot sandwich made with rye bread, sauerkraut, corned beef, Swiss cheese, and Russian dressing. It is typically grilled until the bread is golden and the cheese melts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sandwich was created in the 1920s at Blackstone’s Delicatessen in Omaha, Nebraska.
It is named after the restaurant’s owner, Reuben Kulakofsky.
Traditional recipes use rye bread, though some regions substitute wheat bread.
It is often served with potato chips or pickles on the side.
By the 1940s the Reuben became a staple in U.S. army mess halls.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Corned beef provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat contains heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Probiotic sauerkraut
items.content: Fermented cabbage supplies beneficial bacteria that support gut health.

items.title: Calcium content
items.content: Swiss cheese adds calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and bread supply B12, B6, and niacin, aiding energy metabolism.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Sauerkraut and Russian dressing can be salty, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese and beef contain saturated fats that should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Swiss cheese may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Foodborne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked corned beef can harbor pathogens; it should reach an internal temperature of 63 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place a layer of sauerkraut on a slice of rye bread, add thinly sliced corned beef, top with a slice of Swiss cheese, and drizzle Russian dressing. Grill in a preheated oven at 180 °C for 10‑12 minutes until the cheese melts and the bread is crisp.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The sandwich is best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store it in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep cheese and meat wrapped separately at 0‑4 °C to maintain quality.

turnip-greens-fresh-cooked-fat-added.title: Turnip greens, fresh, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Turnip greens are the leafy tops of the turnip plant, commonly used as a vegetable. When cooked with added fat the leaves stay bright green, become tender, and retain a mildly bitter flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turnip greens belong to the cruciferous family, like broccoli and cabbage.
The leaves are rich in chlorophyll, giving them a deep green color.
In traditional Southern US cuisine they are often prepared as “collard greens” with bacon or ham.
Turnip greens contain more vitamin K than spinach.
They can be used in soups, stews, and as a side dish.

items.title: High in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for normal blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamins A and C
items.content: These vitamins support vision, immunity, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is important for DNA synthesis and especially beneficial during pregnancy.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Glucosinolates and carotenoids help combat free radicals.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Turnip greens contain oxalates, which may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, people allergic to other cruciferous vegetables may react to turnip greens.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Cooking with added fat increases calorie density; monitor the amount of oil or meat used.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turnip greens are typically simmered in a small amount of fat (oil, bacon) until tender, often with onion and garlic. They can also be quickly sautéed or added to soups and stews. Serve hot as a side dish or cooled in salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh leaves in the refrigerator in a perforated bag for 3‑5 days. Cooked turnip greens can be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days or frozen for up to 2 months.
